name: OMK 2A Heme — Summative 3 Objective Review · Board-Style Set 1

questions.stem:
A 58-year-old man comes to the office because of a 4-month history of fatigue and decreased exercise tolerance. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. He does not smoke cigarettes or drink alcoholic beverages, and his diet is unrestricted. His temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg. Physical examination shows conjunctival pallor and spooning of the fingernails. There is no lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly, or splenomegaly. Rectal examination shows no masses, and a test of the stool for occult blood is negative. Laboratory studies show:

    Hemoglobin                      9.2 g/dL
    Hematocrit                      28%
    Mean corpuscular volume         68 μm3
    Red cell distribution width     18.5% (N=11.5–14.5)
    Platelet count                  468,000/mm3
    Reticulocyte count              0.9%
    Serum ferritin                  6 ng/mL
    Serum iron                      22 μg/dL
    Total iron-binding capacity     465 μg/dL

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
choices: A. Administration of intravenous iron sucrose
B. Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy
E. Oral ferrous sulfate therapy alone
F. Repeat testing of the stool for occult blood in 3 months
questions.explanation: Low ferritin + high total iron-binding capacity + high red cell distribution width + microcytosis → iron deficiency, and the reactive thrombocytosis and low reticulocyte count fit. But iron deficiency is a finding, not a diagnosis. In an adult man (or a postmenopausal woman) with no menstrual or dietary explanation, the iron left the body somewhere → occult gastrointestinal blood loss until proven otherwise → colonoscopy. A single negative stool guaiac does not exclude this: gastrointestinal bleeding from a colonic neoplasm is intermittent, and the test is neither sensitive nor designed to overrule an established iron deficit. Replacing the iron without finding the leak treats the number and misses the tumor.

wrongExplanations.0: Intravenous iron would be the answer if the source had already been identified and the patient could not absorb or tolerate oral iron. It corrects the deficit without addressing why an adult man is losing iron.
wrongExplanations.1: Marrow biopsy would be the answer if other cell lines were involved — leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, or a leukoerythroblastic smear with teardrop cells and nucleated red cells. Here the platelets are high and only the red cells are affected, and the iron studies already explain the anemia.
wrongExplanations.3: Hemoglobin electrophoresis would be the answer if the indices pointed to thalassemia trait: a normal or high erythrocyte count, a normal red cell distribution width, and normal iron studies. The low ferritin and high iron-binding capacity here exclude it.
wrongExplanations.4: Oral iron alone would be the answer in a menstruating woman or a patient with a clear dietary cause. Given alone in this patient it would correct the hemoglobin and delay the diagnosis of the lesion that is bleeding.
wrongExplanations.5: Repeating the stool test would be the answer if the pretest probability of a lesion were low. It is not: the iron deficiency itself is the abnormal screening result, and a second negative guaiac would not change the indication for colonoscopy.

questions.eli5: His body is low on iron, and iron does not just vanish — it leaks out with blood. In a grown man there is no normal way to lose blood, so a doctor has to look inside the intestine with a camera to find the leak. Just handing him iron pills would hide the problem instead of finding it.

questions.stem:
A 67-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 5-month history of fatigue and numbness of both feet. She has a 10-year history of hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine. She does not smoke cigarettes or drink alcoholic beverages. Her diet includes meat, eggs, and dairy products. Her temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), pulse is 82/min, and blood pressure is 132/78 mm Hg. Physical examination shows conjunctival pallor and a smooth, beefy red tongue. Sensation to vibration and joint position is decreased over both great toes, and ankle reflexes are absent. Gait is wide-based. Laboratory studies show:

    Hemoglobin                  9.8 g/dL
    Hematocrit                  30%
    Mean corpuscular volume     112 μm3
    Leukocyte count             3,800/mm3
    Platelet count              118,000/mm3
    Reticulocyte count          0.7%
    Lactate dehydrogenase       620 U/L
    Total bilirubin             1.9 mg/dL
    Direct bilirubin            0.3 mg/dL
    Serum vitamin B12           212 pg/mL (N=200–900)

A peripheral blood smear shows oval macrocytes and neutrophils with six or more nuclear lobes. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
choices: C. Measurement of serum folate concentration
D. Measurement of serum homocysteine concentration
E. Measurement of serum methylmalonic acid concentration
F. Measurement of serum thyroid-stimulating hormone concentration
questions.explanation: Macrocytosis + hypersegmented neutrophils + pancytopenia + a low reticulocyte count → megaloblastic anemia from impaired DNA synthesis. The high lactate dehydrogenase and unconjugated bilirubin are not peripheral hemolysis; they are ineffective erythropoiesis — cells dying inside the marrow. The problem is that the B12 level is low-NORMAL, so the assay itself does not settle it, and roughly 40% of true B12 deficiency has a level in this gray zone. Methylmalonic acid is the discriminator: it accumulates ONLY in B12 deficiency (B12 is the cofactor for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase) and is normal in folate deficiency. The clinical stakes are the reason it matters — giving folate to a B12-deficient patient corrects the blood count while subacute combined degeneration of the dorsal and lateral columns marches on toward irreversible.

wrongExplanations.0: Marrow aspiration would be the answer if the smear showed blasts or dysplastic changes suggesting myelodysplastic syndrome. The hypersegmented neutrophils and oval macrocytes already point to a nutritional megaloblastic process that a blood test can confirm.
wrongExplanations.1: A direct antiglobulin test would be the answer if this were hemolysis — a HIGH reticulocyte count with spherocytes. The reticulocyte count of 0.7% shows the marrow is not releasing cells, so the raised lactate dehydrogenase and bilirubin are intramedullary, not immune destruction.
wrongExplanations.2: Serum folate would be the answer if there were no neurologic findings and a dietary or alcohol history suggested folate deficiency. Folate deficiency does not cause the posterior-column signs seen here, and a folate level would not distinguish the two once B12 is equivocal.
wrongExplanations.3: Homocysteine would be the answer if you only needed to confirm that a megaloblastic process exists. It rises in BOTH B12 and folate deficiency, so it cannot discriminate between them — which is precisely what this case requires.
wrongExplanations.5: Thyroid-stimulating hormone would be the answer if the hypothyroidism were untreated and there were no neurologic signs or hypersegmented neutrophils. Hypothyroidism causes a mild macrocytosis without megaloblastic morphology or pancytopenia. Her autoimmune thyroid disease is a clue toward pernicious anemia, not a competing explanation.

questions.eli5: Her red blood cells are too big and her feet are going numb, which points at a missing vitamin. Two different vitamins can make big cells, but only one of them — B12 — also damages nerves. A special test called methylmalonic acid rises only with B12, so it tells the doctor which vitamin is actually missing.

questions.stem:
A 9-year-old boy with hereditary spherocytosis is brought to the emergency department by his mother because of increasing pallor and fatigue for 5 days. He has never required a transfusion. His hemoglobin concentration was 10.5 g/dL at a routine visit 3 months ago. Two weeks ago he had a low-grade fever and a bright red rash over both cheeks that resolved without treatment. His temperature is 37.2°C (99.0°F), pulse is 124/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 96/58 mm Hg. Physical examination shows marked pallor and scleral icterus; the spleen is palpated 4 cm below the left costal margin, unchanged from previous examinations. Laboratory studies show:

    Hemoglobin                          4.8 g/dL
    Hematocrit                          13%
    Mean corpuscular volume             82 μm3
    Mean corpuscular hemoglobin conc.   36.9 g/dL (N=32–36)
    Reticulocyte count                  0.2%
    Leukocyte count                     6,200/mm3
    Platelet count                      240,000/mm3
    Total bilirubin                     2.1 mg/dL
    Direct bilirubin                    0.3 mg/dL
    Haptoglobin                         12 mg/dL (N=30–200)

A peripheral blood smear shows numerous small round erythrocytes lacking central pallor. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's acute decompensation?
choices: B. Autoimmune hemolysis superimposed on the underlying disorder
D. Parvovirus B19 infection of erythroid progenitor cells
questions.explanation: The buried clue is the reticulocyte count of 0.2%. A child with hereditary spherocytosis survives by running his marrow at maximum output; his baseline reticulocyte count should be markedly HIGH. A hemoglobin that has fallen from 10.5 to 4.8 g/dL with essentially no reticulocytes means production has stopped, not that destruction has increased. Parvovirus B19 binds the P antigen on erythroid progenitors and shuts erythropoiesis down for about a week → in a normal person that is unnoticed, but in someone whose red cells only live 10–20 days it is catastrophic. The slapped-cheek rash 2 weeks ago dates the infection. The low haptoglobin and unconjugated bilirubin confirm his chronic hemolysis is still running — he is destroying cells and no longer replacing them.

wrongExplanations.0: Splenic sequestration would be the answer if the spleen had acutely ENLARGED and the platelet count had fallen as platelets were trapped along with the red cells. His spleen is unchanged and his platelet count is normal, and sequestration would not suppress the reticulocyte count.
wrongExplanations.1: Superimposed autoimmune hemolysis would be the answer if the direct antiglobulin test were positive and the reticulocyte count were HIGH. Added destruction drives the marrow harder; it does not silence it.
wrongExplanations.2: Iron deficiency would be the answer if the mean corpuscular volume were low with a low ferritin, and it develops over months rather than 5 days. His mean corpuscular volume is normal and the mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration is high, which is the opposite pattern.
wrongExplanations.4: Transient erythroblastopenia of childhood also produces anemia with a low reticulocyte count, and it is the closest competitor. It would be the answer in a previously healthy child with NO underlying hemolytic disorder and no preceding parvovirus illness. The known spherocytosis and the slapped-cheek rash place this case with parvovirus.

questions.eli5: His red blood cells break apart faster than normal, so his bone marrow has to work overtime forever just to keep up. A virus came along and shut that factory down for about a week. A healthy person would not notice, but he ran out of red cells almost immediately.

questions.stem:
A 24-year-old woman comes to the office for a routine health maintenance examination. She feels well and has no symptoms. A mild anemia has been noted on several previous complete blood counts, and she has taken oral iron intermittently for 2 years with no change in her hemoglobin concentration. Menses occur at regular 28-day intervals and last 4 days. She has no history of serious illness. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Laboratory studies show:

    Hemoglobin                      11.2 g/dL
    Hematocrit                      34%
    Erythrocyte count               5.5 million/mm3
    Mean corpuscular volume         62 μm3
    Red cell distribution width     13.1% (N=11.5–14.5)
    Platelet count                  244,000/mm3

A peripheral blood smear shows small pale erythrocytes and numerous cells with a central dense area surrounded by a pale ring. Iron studies are pending; the columns below are, in order:

    Serum iron | Total iron-binding capacity | Serum ferritin | Transferrin saturation

Which of the following sets of results is most likely in this patient?
questions.explanation: Three findings say this is not iron deficiency. The erythrocyte COUNT is high-normal at 5.5 million despite a mean corpuscular volume of 62 — a thalassemic marrow makes plenty of cells, each of them small, whereas an iron-starved marrow cannot make enough cells at all. The red cell distribution width is NORMAL: iron deficiency produces a mixed population of old normal cells and new small ones, so the width widens. And 2 years of iron produced no response. Mentzer index = mean corpuscular volume / erythrocyte count = 62/5.5 = 11.3, and under 13 favors thalassemia trait. Target cells fit. In thalassemia trait the iron handling is entirely normal — the defect is in globin chain production, not iron supply → all four iron studies are normal. The management point is that she should be given NOTHING, and specifically not more iron.

wrongExplanations.0: This row is anemia of inflammation: iron and iron-binding capacity both LOW with ferritin high, because hepcidin locks iron inside macrophages and ferritin rises as an acute-phase reactant. It would be the answer if she had a chronic inflammatory, infectious, or malignant disease.
wrongExplanations.1: This row is iron deficiency: low iron, HIGH binding capacity (the liver makes more transferrin when iron is scarce), low ferritin. It would be the answer if the red cell distribution width were high, the erythrocyte count low, and the anemia had responded to 2 years of iron.
wrongExplanations.2: This row is iron overload — hereditary hemochromatosis or sideroblastic anemia. It would be the answer with a high transferrin saturation and, for sideroblastic anemia, ringed sideroblasts on iron staining of the marrow.
wrongExplanations.3: This row is deliberately correct in the first two columns and wrong in the last two — it is what you get by knowing that thalassemia does not disturb serum iron but forgetting that it does not disturb the storage pool either. A low ferritin means iron deficiency, which this patient does not have.

questions.eli5: Her red blood cells are small, but she is not short of iron — she has an inherited difference in how she builds the protein inside them. Her body actually makes plenty of cells, just tiny ones. Giving her more iron does nothing and, if it keeps being given, can slowly overload her.

questions.stem:
A 34-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 3-week history of fatigue and shortness of breath on climbing stairs. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. Her mother and a maternal uncle each underwent splenectomy in early adulthood for anemia. Her temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse is 104/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg. Physical examination shows scleral icterus and conjunctival pallor; the spleen is palpated 3 cm below the left costal margin. Laboratory studies show:

    Hemoglobin                  8.1 g/dL
    Hematocrit                  24%
    Mean corpuscular volume     94 μm3
    Reticulocyte count          9.4%
    Platelet count              232,000/mm3
    Lactate dehydrogenase       512 U/L
    Total bilirubin             3.4 mg/dL
    Direct bilirubin            0.4 mg/dL
    Haptoglobin                 Undetectable (N=30–200 mg/dL)

A peripheral blood smear shows numerous small round erythrocytes lacking central pallor. A direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test is positive for IgG. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Reticulocytosis + unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia + high lactate dehydrogenase + undetectable haptoglobin → hemolysis, and the preserved platelet count with splenomegaly makes it extravascular. The smear narrows it to a spherocytic process, and there are only two common ones. The direct antiglobulin test is the single test that settles it: POSITIVE means antibody is coating the cells and the spleen is stripping their membranes off → immune-mediated hemolysis. NEGATIVE would mean the membrane skeleton itself is defective → hereditary spherocytosis. Same smear, opposite disease. The family history of splenectomy for anemia is the dramatic decoy — it surface-reads toward the inherited disorder, and the antibody result overrules it.

wrongExplanations.1: G6PD deficiency would be the answer with bite cells and Heinz bodies after an oxidant exposure — a drug, fava beans, or an infection — and the direct antiglobulin test would be negative. It is also X-linked and would be unusual in a woman.
wrongExplanations.2: Hereditary elliptocytosis would be the answer if the smear showed cigar-shaped elliptical cells rather than spherocytes, and most patients are asymptomatic rather than anemic.
wrongExplanations.3: Hereditary spherocytosis is the near-miss and fits everything EXCEPT the antibody test — it requires a NEGATIVE direct antiglobulin test. That single result is what separates the two, and here it is positive.
wrongExplanations.4: Microangiopathic hemolysis would be the answer if the smear showed fragmented helmet-shaped schistocytes and the platelet count were LOW from consumption. Her platelets are normal and her cells are spherical, not fragmented.
wrongExplanations.5: Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria would be the answer with INTRAVASCULAR hemolysis — hemoglobinuria, urine hemosiderin — and absent CD55 and CD59 on flow cytometry, with a negative antiglobulin test.
wrongExplanations.6: Pyruvate kinase deficiency would be the answer with a nonspherocytic hemolytic anemia present from childhood and a negative antiglobulin test; it produces no diagnostic morphology on the smear.

questions.eli5: Her immune system is putting sticky tags on her own red blood cells, and her spleen chews the tagged cells until they turn into little balls. An inherited disease makes identical-looking balls, so the smear alone cannot tell them apart. One test that looks for the tags gives the answer.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man is receiving his second unit of packed red blood cells for anemia on the third day after a total hip arthroplasty. Ninety minutes into the transfusion he becomes acutely short of breath. He has a history of hypertension treated with amlodipine and has no history of heart failure. He has received no intravenous fluids other than the transfusion. His temperature is 38.1°C (100.6°F), pulse is 112/min, respirations are 30/min, and blood pressure is 84/52 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 84%. Jugular venous pressure is not elevated. Auscultation of the chest shows diffuse crackles over both lung fields. A chest x-ray shows bilateral pulmonary opacities without cardiomegaly. Administration of furosemide produces a brisk diuresis with no improvement in oxygenation. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Hypoxia + bilateral opacities within 6 hours of a transfusion is the picture of acute respiratory distress syndrome, and there are exactly two transfusion causes. Three findings pick between them: the blood pressure is LOW, the jugular venous pressure is NORMAL, and diuresis does NOT help. That is transfusion-related acute lung injury — donor anti-HLA antibodies (classically from a multiparous female donor, since 14–20% of women who have been pregnant carry them) react with recipient leukocytes, which agglutinate in the pulmonary capillaries → an immune injury to the alveolar-capillary membrane. It is an injury, not a volume problem, so removing volume cannot fix it.

wrongExplanations.0: An acute hemolytic reaction would be the answer with back and flank pain, pink plasma, hemoglobinuria, and a positive direct antiglobulin test — the intravascular hemolysis signature. It also occurs within minutes and is dose-dependent, not 90 minutes in.
wrongExplanations.1: Anaphylaxis would be the answer with urticaria, throat tightness, and hypotension after a TINY volume (classically 5 mL) in an IgA-deficient recipient with anti-IgA antibodies. It does not produce bilateral pulmonary opacities or fever.
wrongExplanations.2: A febrile nonhemolytic reaction would be the answer if fever and chills were the ONLY findings, from donor leukocyte cytokines. It is self-limited and does not cause hypoxemia or an abnormal chest film.
wrongExplanations.3: A septic reaction would be the answer with rigors and rapid circulatory collapse, most often after a PLATELET unit — platelets are stored at room temperature, so contaminating skin flora multiply. It would not produce this isolated bilateral pulmonary picture with a response to nothing but time.
wrongExplanations.4: Circulatory overload is the near-miss and looks identical on the chest film. It is flipped by three findings, all of which point the other way here: the blood pressure would be HIGH, the jugular venous pressure RAISED, and diuresis WOULD help.

questions.eli5: The donated blood carried antibodies that attacked the white blood cells in his lungs, and the lungs filled with fluid from that injury. It looks exactly like having too much fluid in the body, but the fix for too much fluid — a water pill — did nothing. His low blood pressure and flat neck veins say it was an injury, not extra volume.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman is receiving a transfusion of packed red blood cells for symptomatic anemia. She shares a semiprivate room with another patient, and both are cared for by the same nurse. Ten minutes into the unit she develops severe back and flank pain, fever, and rigors. Her temperature is 39.0°C (102.2°F), pulse is 128/min, respirations are 26/min, and blood pressure is 78/44 mm Hg. The transfusion is stopped immediately. Her plasma appears pink and her urine is dark red. A direct antiglobulin test performed on a post-transfusion sample is positive. Repeat typing shows the patient is blood group O; the transfused unit was group A. The blood bank confirms that its own typing of the pretransfusion sample it received was performed correctly. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this event?
choices: A. Delayed anamnestic response to a minor erythrocyte antigen from prior sensitization
B. Failure to irradiate the unit before it was released by the blood bank
C. Failure to leukocyte-reduce the unit before it was released by the blood bank
D. Misidentification of the patient at the time of the pretransfusion sample draw
E. Passive transfer of anti-HLA antibodies present in the donor's plasma
questions.explanation: Naturally occurring IgM anti-A in a group O recipient fixes complement on transfused group A cells → INTRAVASCULAR lysis → hemoglobinemia (pink plasma), hemoglobinuria (dark red urine), and a positive direct antiglobulin test, with the characteristic back and flank pain. The question asks one step back: why did a group O patient receive group A blood? The blood bank typed its sample correctly, so the error happened BEFORE the sample reached it — 'wrong blood in tube.' A nurse holding pre-printed labels for two roommates draws the tube from one patient and applies the other's label. The blood bank then types the wrong person's blood flawlessly, and everything downstream is perfectly, consistently wrong. This is why the clerical check comparing unit label to patient identity is step 3 of the transfusion reaction algorithm, and why bedside labeling is treated as a never event.

wrongExplanations.0: A delayed anamnestic response would be the answer 2–10 days after transfusion, with a gradual fall in hemoglobin from an antibody to a minor antigen such as Kidd or Rh. It is extravascular and does not produce hemoglobinuria minutes into the unit.
wrongExplanations.1: Failure to irradiate would be the answer for transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease, which appears 1–6 weeks later with pancytopenia, rash, diarrhea, and liver dysfunction. Irradiation has no bearing on ABO compatibility.
wrongExplanations.2: Failure to leukocyte-reduce would be the answer for a febrile nonhemolytic reaction, in which donor leukocyte cytokines cause fever and chills with NO hemolysis. Leukoreduction does nothing to prevent an ABO error.
wrongExplanations.4: Passive transfer of donor anti-HLA antibodies would be the answer for transfusion-related acute lung injury — hypoxia with bilateral pulmonary opacities. It does not cause red cell lysis or hemoglobinuria.

questions.eli5: Blood comes in types, and giving someone the wrong type makes their body destroy the new blood instantly. The lab did its job perfectly — it just tested a tube of blood that came from the wrong person. Two patients in one room with two sets of labels is how that mix-up happens.

questions.stem:
A 74-year-old woman is admitted to the hospital for evaluation of a 2-month history of fatigue. A complete blood count obtained on a specimen collected in the emergency department and transported through an unheated ambulance bay shows:

    Hemoglobin                          10.4 g/dL
    Hematocrit                          22%
    Erythrocyte count                   2.1 million/mm3
    Mean corpuscular volume             105 μm3
    Mean corpuscular hemoglobin conc.   47 g/dL (N=32–36)
    Leukocyte count                     6,800/mm3
    Platelet count                      210,000/mm3

She is hemodynamically stable and has no bleeding. Physical examination shows mild conjunctival pallor and no other abnormalities. A peripheral blood smear prepared at room temperature shows clumping of erythrocytes into irregular aggregates. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluation of these results?
choices: A. Measurement of the serum ferritin and transferrin saturation
B. Redrawing the specimen into a citrate-containing tube and repeating the count
C. Repeating the complete blood count after warming the specimen to 37°C
D. Reporting the results as measured and repeating them in one week
E. Transfusion of packed erythrocytes for the reported hematocrit
questions.explanation: The analyzer measures only three things — erythrocyte count, mean corpuscular volume, and hemoglobin — and calculates the rest. Cold agglutinins clump red cells, so the instrument counts each CLUMP as one large cell: the erythrocyte count reads falsely LOW and the mean corpuscular volume falsely HIGH. Check the arithmetic: hematocrit = erythrocyte count x mean corpuscular volume / 10 = 2.1 x 105/10 = 22%, so the falsely low count propagates into a falsely low hematocrit. Hemoglobin is measured on LYSED cells, so it is unaffected at 10.4. Mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration = hemoglobin/hematocrit x 100 = 10.4/22 x 100 = 47 g/dL. Any value above about 37 g/dL is an artefact, because a red cell physically cannot hold that much hemoglobin. The tell is that the hemoglobin is not roughly one third of the hematocrit. Warming the specimen to 37°C disperses the agglutinins and the indices correct.

wrongExplanations.0: Ferritin would be the answer if the indices were believable and pointed to a microcytic anemia. Here the indices are internally impossible, so no result should be interpreted until the artefact is removed.
wrongExplanations.1: A citrate tube is the correct fix for a different artefact — EDTA-dependent platelet clumping causing pseudothrombocytopenia. It addresses PLATELET clumping; her platelet count is normal and the aggregates on this smear are erythrocytes.
wrongExplanations.3: Reporting as measured would be the answer only if the values were internally consistent. A mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration of 47 g/dL is not a physiologic value, and acting on the hematocrit of 22% would mean treating a number the instrument invented.
wrongExplanations.4: Transfusion would be the answer if the true hematocrit were 22% in a symptomatic patient. Her real hemoglobin is 10.4 g/dL and she is stable — transfusing here would expose her to risk for an anemia she does not have.

questions.eli5: Her blood got cold on the way to the lab, and the cells stuck together in little clumps. The machine counted each clump as one giant cell, so it thought she had far fewer cells than she does. Warming the sample back up unsticks them and gives the real numbers.

questions.stem:
A 6-year-old girl who is receiving induction chemotherapy for acute lymphoblastic leukemia is brought to the clinic by her father for a scheduled visit. She feels well and has had no fever, cough, or dysuria. Her temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse is 92/min, and blood pressure is 98/60 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no abnormalities; there is no mucositis and no erythema, tenderness, or discharge at the central venous catheter exit site. Laboratory studies show:

    Leukocyte count             1,200/mm3
      Segmented neutrophils     12%
      Band forms                3%
      Lymphocytes               78%
      Monocytes                 7%

Which of the following is this patient's absolute neutrophil count?
questions.explanation: Absolute neutrophil count = leukocyte count x (% segmented neutrophils + % band forms) = 1,200 x (12 + 3)/100 = 1,200 x 0.15 = 180/mm3. Bands are counted because they are functional neutrophils. The count must be ABSOLUTE, never a percentage — a 12% neutrophil fraction means something completely different at a leukocyte count of 1,200 than at 12,000. The thresholds: below 1,000/mm3 infection risk climbs; below 500/mm3 the patient cannot contain their own flora; below 200/mm3 there is essentially NO inflammatory response, which is why this child's reassuring examination is not reassuring at all. With no neutrophils there is nothing to make pus, redness, or an infiltrate, so fever may be the only sign an infection ever produces — and the absent mucositis and clean catheter site here are exactly the findings that cannot be trusted.

wrongExplanations.0: 144/mm3 uses the segmented neutrophils alone (1,200 x 0.12) and omits the band forms. Bands are mature enough to fight infection and are included in the calculation.
wrongExplanations.1: 15/mm3 is the sum of the percentages (12 + 3) reported as though it were a count. This is the single commonest error — treating a percentage as an absolute number.
wrongExplanations.3: 264/mm3 adds the monocytes (12 + 3 + 7 = 22%). Monocytes contribute to host defense but are not part of the absolute NEUTROPHIL count.
wrongExplanations.4: 936/mm3 uses the lymphocyte percentage (1,200 x 0.78). Her lymphocytes are the majority of a small total, which is why the neutrophil fraction looks deceptively minor.

questions.eli5: Percentages can fool you: 12% of a small number is still a very small number. Multiplying gives about 180 infection-fighting cells, when a healthy child has thousands. With so few, she cannot make redness or pus, so a fever might be the only warning sign she ever gets.

questions.stem:
A 29-year-old woman comes to the office for evaluation of an abnormal laboratory result found during preoperative testing before an elective cholecystectomy. She has never had abnormal bleeding, including after a wisdom tooth extraction and two vaginal deliveries. She has had two spontaneous abortions, at 11 and 14 weeks' gestation. Six months ago she was treated for a deep venous thrombosis of the left calf that occurred without an identifiable provoking factor. She takes no medications and has received no heparin. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows no abnormalities; there are no petechiae or ecchymoses. Laboratory studies show:

    Platelet count                              132,000/mm3
    Prothrombin time                            12 sec (N=11–14)
    Activated partial thromboplastin time       58 sec (N=25–35)

A 1:1 mixing study with normal plasma does not correct the activated partial thromboplastin time. The activated partial thromboplastin time corrects with the addition of excess phospholipid. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for these findings?
choices: E. Heparin contamination of the specimen
questions.explanation: The mixing study is the fork in the road: adding normal plasma supplies roughly 50% of every factor, and 30% activity is enough to clot. So if a FACTOR IS MISSING the time corrects; if something is BLOCKING the reaction it stays prolonged. Here it stays prolonged → an inhibitor. The second test names which inhibitor: adding excess phospholipid corrects it, meaning the antibody was competing for phospholipid rather than attacking a factor. That is a lupus anticoagulant, and the name is wrong on both counts — most patients do not have lupus, and it is not an anticoagulant. It prolongs clotting IN VITRO by soaking up the phospholipid the assay depends on, while causing thrombosis IN VIVO. Her clinical history confirms it: unprovoked thrombosis, two second-trimester losses, mild thrombocytopenia, and NO bleeding despite a markedly prolonged time. Diagnosis requires persistence on repeat testing 12 weeks apart plus a clinical criterion.

wrongExplanations.0: An acquired factor VIII inhibitor is the near-miss — it also fails to correct on mixing. It is flipped by two things: adding excess phospholipid would NOT correct it, and the patient would BLEED, often catastrophically, rather than clot. Detecting a slow factor VIII antibody also requires incubating the mix 30–60 minutes at 37°C.
wrongExplanations.2: Factor XII deficiency prolongs the activated partial thromboplastin time and causes NO bleeding, which fits her history nicely — but it is a deficiency, so the mixing study would CORRECT. It also does not cause thrombosis or fetal loss.
wrongExplanations.3: A hemophilia A carrier would have a normal or only mildly prolonged time that CORRECTS on mixing, and if symptomatic at all would bleed rather than clot.
wrongExplanations.4: Heparin contamination (typically from a line draw) also fails to correct on mixing, and would be the answer if the thrombin time were prolonged and corrected in the presence of a heparin-neutralizing agent. She has received no heparin, and the phospholipid correction points elsewhere.

questions.eli5: Her blood took a long time to clot in the test tube, but she has never had a bleeding problem — she has had clots and lost pregnancies. An antibody is soaking up an ingredient the test needs, so the test looks abnormal while her body actually clots too much. Adding more of that ingredient fixes the test and reveals what the antibody was doing.

questions.stem:
A 19-year-old woman comes to the office because of heavy menstrual bleeding since menarche and frequent nosebleeds. She required nasal packing twice during adolescence. Her father has a similar history of nosebleeds and bled excessively after a dental extraction. She has never had bleeding into a joint or muscle. She takes no medications. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows scattered ecchymoses over both shins; there is no joint swelling or deformity. Laboratory studies show:

    Platelet count                                  178,000/mm3
    Prothrombin time                                12 sec (N=11–14)
    Activated partial thromboplastin time           34 sec (N=25–35)
    von Willebrand factor antigen                   62% (N=50–150)
    von Willebrand factor ristocetin cofactor       22% (N=50–150)
    Factor VIII activity                            74% (N=50–150)

Which of the following best explains this patient's bleeding disorder?
choices: A. A qualitative defect in von Willebrand factor
B. A quantitative deficiency of von Willebrand factor
E. Impaired platelet aggregation caused by a glycoprotein IIb/IIIa defect
questions.explanation: Two readings matter. First, WHERE she bleeds: mucocutaneous bleeding — nose, gums, menorrhagia, bruising — points to platelets or von Willebrand factor, whereas joint and muscle bleeding points to hemophilia. Second, the ANTIGEN-TO-ACTIVITY comparison, which is von Willebrand disease in one question. The antigen is 62% — she has a normal AMOUNT of protein. The ristocetin cofactor activity is 22% — the protein she has does not WORK. The ratio is 22/62 = 0.35, and below about 0.5–0.7 defines a QUALITATIVE defect (type 2), from loss of the high-molecular-weight multimers that do the actual platelet tethering. Note also that her activated partial thromboplastin time is completely NORMAL: PT and aPTT are plasma assays run after the platelets were spun out, so von Willebrand disease and platelet function defects are invisible to them. Von Willebrand testing must be requested separately. The treatment consequence is real — desmopressin works for type 1, but type 2B and type 3 need factor concentrate instead.

wrongExplanations.1: A quantitative deficiency (type 1 or type 3) is the near-miss and the more common form. It would be the answer if antigen and activity fell TOGETHER, keeping the ratio near 1. Her antigen is normal while her activity is a third of it, so the molecule is defective rather than scarce.
wrongExplanations.2: Factor VIII deficiency would be the answer with a prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time, bleeding into joints and muscles, and an X-linked pattern. Her factor VIII is 74% and her aPTT is normal, and her father — not just her maternal relatives — is affected.
wrongExplanations.3: Factor XIII deficiency is the disorder in which every screening test is normal, so it is a genuine consideration whenever PT, aPTT, and platelet count are all unremarkable. It is excluded here by the abnormal ristocetin cofactor activity, and it classically causes DELAYED bleeding and umbilical stump bleeding at birth.
wrongExplanations.4: A glycoprotein IIb/IIIa defect (Glanzmann thrombasthenia) also causes mucocutaneous bleeding with normal clotting times, and would be the answer if platelet aggregation studies were abnormal to every agonist EXCEPT ristocetin, with normal von Willebrand studies. Here the von Willebrand studies are the abnormality.

questions.eli5: Von Willebrand factor is the glue that sticks platelets to a wound. She has a normal amount of glue, but her glue does not stick — that is why the amount looks fine and the function test is low. The usual clotting tests miss this completely, so it has to be asked for on purpose.

questions.stem:
A 31-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her husband because of confusion and headache for 1 day. He says she has been increasingly withdrawn for 3 days. She takes no medications and has had no diarrhea. Her temperature is 38.0°C (100.4°F), pulse is 108/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 138/84 mm Hg. She is oriented to person only. There is no nuchal rigidity and no focal neurologic deficit. Scattered petechiae are present over both lower extremities. Laboratory studies show:

    Hemoglobin                                  7.6 g/dL
    Hematocrit                                  23%
    Platelet count                              14,000/mm3
    Reticulocyte count                          7.2%
    Lactate dehydrogenase                       1,480 U/L
    Total bilirubin                             3.1 mg/dL
    Direct bilirubin                            0.3 mg/dL
    Haptoglobin                                 Undetectable (N=30–200 mg/dL)
    Serum creatinine                            1.3 mg/dL
    Prothrombin time                            12 sec (N=11–14)
    Activated partial thromboplastin time       30 sec (N=25–35)
    Fibrinogen                                  340 mg/dL (N=200–400)

A direct antiglobulin test is negative. A peripheral blood smear shows numerous fragmented erythrocytes with angular, helmet-shaped outlines. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
choices: B. Administration of intravenous immune globulin
questions.explanation: Schistocytes + thrombocytopenia + a hemolysis panel that moves as a unit (high lactate dehydrogenase, undetectable haptoglobin, unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, high reticulocytes) with a NEGATIVE antiglobulin test = a thrombotic microangiopathy. The coagulation panel is the discriminator, not the smear: PT, aPTT, and fibrinogen are all NORMAL, which excludes disseminated intravascular coagulation. Among the microangiopathies, neurologic predominance with near-normal renal function means brain, not kidney → thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura from ADAMTS13 failure, usually an acquired IgG inhibitor in a patient in her 20s or 30s. Uncleaved ultra-large von Willebrand factor multimers act as adhesive ropes that seize platelets everywhere. Untreated mortality exceeds 90%, so plasma exchange is started on clinical suspicion, BEFORE the ADAMTS13 level returns. Exchange does two things at once — the plasma given back replaces the enzyme, and the plasma removed takes the autoantibody with it.

wrongExplanations.0: Eculizumab is the treatment for atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome, which would be the answer with unregulated complement activation and PREDOMINANTLY RENAL injury. Her creatinine is 1.3 mg/dL and her presentation is neurologic; genotyping matters there before any kidney transplant.
wrongExplanations.1: Intravenous immune globulin would be the answer for immune thrombocytopenic purpura — ISOLATED thrombocytopenia with a normal hemoglobin, no schistocytes, and no hemolysis. She has a full microangiopathic hemolytic anemia.
wrongExplanations.2: Antibiotics would be the answer if sepsis with disseminated intravascular coagulation were causing this, which would require a PROLONGED PT and aPTT with a FALLING fibrinogen. All three are normal, which is exactly what excludes it.
wrongExplanations.4: Platelet transfusion is the trap, and it is actively harmful. The thrombocytopenia is CONSUMPTIVE — platelets are being spent in ongoing microvascular thrombosis — so transfusing them adds fuel to the fire. Platelets are withheld in suspected thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura unless there is life-threatening bleeding.

questions.eli5: An enzyme that normally trims long sticky strands in her blood vessels has stopped working, so the strands are catching platelets everywhere and shredding red cells as they squeeze past. Swapping her plasma for donor plasma both replaces the missing enzyme and washes out the antibody attacking it. Giving her platelets would just feed the clots.

questions.stem:
A 66-year-old man is in the hospital on the seventh day after an elective total knee arthroplasty. He has received subcutaneous unfractionated heparin for thromboprophylaxis since the day of surgery. He now has swelling and pain of the right calf. He has had no bleeding, and there is no blood in the surgical drain. His temperature is 37.3°C (99.1°F), pulse is 92/min, and blood pressure is 134/80 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a swollen, tender right calf. The surgical wound is clean and dry. Laboratory studies show:

    Platelet count, on admission                265,000/mm3
    Platelet count, today                       82,000/mm3
    Hemoglobin                                  11.8 g/dL
    Prothrombin time                            12 sec (N=11–14)
    Activated partial thromboplastin time       32 sec (N=25–35)
    Fibrinogen                                  380 mg/dL (N=200–400)

Duplex ultrasonography shows a nonocclusive thrombus in the right popliteal vein. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
choices: A. Continue unfractionated heparin and transfuse platelets
B. Discontinue heparin and begin argatroban
C. Discontinue heparin and begin warfarin
E. Replace unfractionated heparin with enoxaparin
questions.explanation: A platelet count that falls more than 50% on day 5–10 of heparin, in a patient who is CLOTTING rather than bleeding, is heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. Antibodies against the heparin–platelet factor 4 complex bind and ACTIVATE platelets → massive thrombin generation. The name is actively misleading: the platelet count is the clue, but thrombosis is the danger. Normal PT, aPTT, and fibrinogen exclude disseminated intravascular coagulation. Management has two halves and both are required — stop ALL heparin exposure, and start an alternative anticoagulant, because this patient already has a thrombus and the prothrombotic state does not resolve just because the drug is withdrawn. A direct thrombin inhibitor such as argatroban (or bivalirudin, or fondaparinux) is the appropriate choice.

wrongExplanations.0: Continuing heparin leaves the trigger in place, and transfusing platelets treats a number rather than a disease — the platelets are being consumed by activation, and adding more supplies substrate for further thrombosis. He is not bleeding, so there is no indication for platelets at all.
wrongExplanations.2: Warfarin alone is the classic error here. Warfarin depletes protein C and protein S FIRST, because they have the shortest half-lives among the vitamin K-dependent proteins, so it begins by deepening a prothrombotic state — in this setting that risks venous limb gangrene and skin necrosis. Warfarin is added only after the platelet count has recovered and a parenteral agent is established.
wrongExplanations.3: Stopping heparin without starting an alternative would be the answer if there were thrombocytopenia and NO thrombosis and no high clinical probability — and even then most patients are anticoagulated. He has a documented popliteal vein thrombus, which must be treated.
wrongExplanations.4: Low-molecular-weight heparin cross-reacts with the same heparin–platelet factor 4 antibodies. Switching to enoxaparin continues the exposure that caused the problem.

questions.eli5: A blood thinner made his immune system build antibodies that switch platelets ON instead of off. His platelet count dropped, but the real danger is that he is forming clots. Stopping the drug is only half the fix — he needs a completely different kind of blood thinner right away.

questions.stem:
A 38-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of a 2-week history of fatigue, bleeding from the gums when she brushes her teeth, and easy bruising. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. Her temperature is 37.8°C (100.0°F), pulse is 104/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 112/68 mm Hg. Physical examination shows gingival oozing, scattered ecchymoses over the trunk and extremities, and petechiae on the palate. There is no lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly, or splenomegaly. Laboratory studies show:

    Hemoglobin                                  8.4 g/dL
    Hematocrit                                  25%
    Leukocyte count                             1,800/mm3
    Platelet count                              22,000/mm3
    Prothrombin time                            19 sec (N=11–14)
    Activated partial thromboplastin time       44 sec (N=25–35)
    Fibrinogen                                  88 mg/dL (N=200–400)
    D-dimer                                     Markedly increased

A peripheral blood smear shows abnormal promyelocytes with heavy azurophilic granulation, several of which contain multiple needle-shaped inclusions arranged in bundles. Cytogenetic studies are pending. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
choices: A. Administration of all-trans retinoic acid
C. Administration of intravenous immune globulin
D. Initiation of induction chemotherapy with cytarabine and daunorubicin once cytogenetic studies return
questions.explanation: Hypergranular promyelocytes with bundled needle-shaped inclusions (faggot cells packed with Auer rods) plus a florid coagulopathy — prolonged PT and aPTT, fibrinogen falling to 88 mg/dL, D-dimer high — is acute promyelocytic leukemia with disseminated intravascular coagulation. The granules of the malignant promyelocytes are loaded with procoagulant and fibrinolytic material, and when the cells lyse they dump it into the circulation. This is the one leukemia treated on SUSPICION rather than on confirmation: all-trans retinoic acid is started before the t(15;17)/PML-RARA result returns, because the coagulopathy kills within days and retinoic acid begins reversing it almost immediately by driving the promyelocytes to differentiate instead of lysing them. Recognized and treated early, survival is about 90%; the deaths are almost all early hemorrhagic deaths in patients whose treatment waited.

wrongExplanations.1: Imatinib would be the answer for a BCR-ABL1-positive disease — chronic myeloid leukemia or Philadelphia chromosome-positive acute lymphoblastic leukemia. The smear here shows hypergranular promyelocytes, not a full myeloid maturation series with basophilia.
wrongExplanations.2: Intravenous immune globulin would be the answer for immune thrombocytopenic purpura: an ISOLATED low platelet count with normal clotting times, normal fibrinogen, and a normal smear. Her PT, aPTT, and fibrinogen are all deranged and she has circulating abnormal promyelocytes.
wrongExplanations.3: This is the trap. Standard induction is reasonable therapy for other subtypes of acute myeloid leukemia, but WAITING for cytogenetics is the error — the delay is measured against a coagulopathy that causes fatal intracranial or pulmonary hemorrhage within days. Cytotoxic therapy alone also lyses the promyelocytes and can worsen the bleeding.
wrongExplanations.4: Plasma exchange would be the answer for thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, which requires schistocytes with NORMAL PT, aPTT, and fibrinogen. Here the clotting times are prolonged and the fibrinogen is consumed, which is the opposite pattern.

questions.eli5: Her leukemia cells are stuffed with granules that set off uncontrolled clotting and bleeding the moment they break open. That bleeding can kill her within days, faster than any lab result comes back. So the doctor starts a vitamin A-based drug immediately on suspicion, which makes the cells grow up instead of bursting.

questions.stem:
A 52-year-old man comes to the office because of a 4-month history of early satiety, left upper abdominal fullness, and fatigue. He has had no fever, cough, dysuria, or recent illness, and he has not received corticosteroids. He takes no medications. His temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), pulse is 78/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 126/78 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a spleen palpated 8 cm below the left costal margin. There is no lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies show:

    Hemoglobin                  11.6 g/dL
    Leukocyte count             86,000/mm3
      Segmented neutrophils     48%
      Band forms                14%
      Metamyelocytes            12%
      Myelocytes                15%
      Promyelocytes             3%
      Blasts                    2%
      Basophils                 5%
      Eosinophils               1%
    Platelet count              620,000/mm3

A peripheral blood smear shows the full range of granulocyte maturation stages. There is no toxic granulation and there are no Döhle bodies. Which of the following studies is most likely to establish the diagnosis?
choices: A. Cytogenetic and molecular testing for BCR-ABL1
B. Flow cytometry for CD5 and CD23
C. Measurement of the leukocyte alkaline phosphatase score
E. Testing for the JAK2 V617F mutation
questions.explanation: A leukocyte count of 86,000/mm3 with the whole myeloid series present raises two possibilities: chronic myeloid leukemia or a leukemoid reaction. Three findings here favor the neoplasm. BASOPHILIA of 5% is the distinctive finding and does not occur in a reactive process. There is NO trigger — no infection, inflammation, tissue necrosis, or corticosteroid. And there is no toxic granulation and there are no Döhle bodies, the reactive changes of a neutrophil working hard; a leukemoid reaction shows mature neutrophils with those changes and a left shift WITHOUT blasts. Massive splenomegaly and thrombocytosis fit chronic myeloid leukemia. The definitive test is the molecular one: t(9;22) creating BCR-ABL1. Everything else is supportive; the molecular result is diagnostic, and it also selects the treatment, since BCR-ABL1 is the target of imatinib.

wrongExplanations.1: CD5 and CD23 flow cytometry is the workup for a CD5-positive B-cell neoplasm — chronic LYMPHOCYTIC leukemia versus mantle cell lymphoma. It would be the answer if the excess cells were mature lymphocytes with smudge cells, not granulocytes.
wrongExplanations.2: The leukocyte alkaline phosphatase score is the near-miss: it is LOW in chronic myeloid leukemia and HIGH in a leukemoid reaction, so it points in the right direction. But it is a supportive, historical test that is neither definitive nor targetable, and it has been superseded by BCR-ABL1 testing.
wrongExplanations.3: Serum protein electrophoresis looks for a monoclonal paraprotein in myeloma or Waldenström macroglobulinemia, which would present with rouleaux, anemia, renal impairment, or bone pain — not a granulocytic leukocytosis.
wrongExplanations.4: JAK2 V617F is the driver in polycythemia vera, essential thrombocythemia, and primary myelofibrosis. It would be the answer with an elevated hemoglobin, an isolated thrombocytosis, or a leukoerythroblastic smear with teardrop cells. His hemoglobin is low-normal and the full granulocyte series with basophilia points to BCR-ABL1 instead.

questions.eli5: His white blood cell count is enormous, which can mean either a bad infection or a blood cancer. There is no infection to explain it, and he has a specific cell type — basophils — that only goes up in the cancer. A gene test for a swapped piece of two chromosomes gives the definite answer and also names the drug that treats it.

questions.stem:
A 68-year-old man comes to the office because of painless enlargement of lymph nodes on both sides of his neck for 3 months. He has had no fever, drenching night sweats, or weight loss. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. His temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F), pulse is 76/min, and blood pressure is 138/82 mm Hg. Physical examination shows nontender bilateral cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy; the spleen is palpated 2 cm below the left costal margin. Laboratory studies show:

    Hemoglobin              12.8 g/dL
    Leukocyte count         42,000/mm3
      Lymphocytes           82%
    Platelet count          190,000/mm3

A peripheral blood smear shows small mature-appearing lymphocytes with scant cytoplasm and coarse clumped chromatin, together with numerous ruptured cells. Flow cytometry of peripheral blood shows a monoclonal B-cell population expressing CD19, CD20, CD5, and CD23. Cyclin D1 is not expressed. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: CD19 and CD20 establish a B-cell lineage, and monoclonality establishes malignancy. The decisive finding is CD5 — a T-cell marker — on a B cell. Only two B-cell neoplasms do this, and CD23 splits them: CD23 POSITIVE is chronic lymphocytic leukemia; CD23 NEGATIVE with cyclin D1 and t(11;14) is mantle cell lymphoma. Everything else fits: an elderly patient, an absolute lymphocytosis of mature-appearing cells, painless generalized lymphadenopathy, no B symptoms, and the ruptured cells on the smear are smudge cells — fragile lymphocytes crushed during slide preparation. The distinction carries real prognostic weight, since chronic lymphocytic leukemia is indolent and often merely watched, while mantle cell lymphoma is the one where essentially everyone relapses.

wrongExplanations.0: Burkitt lymphoma would be the answer with a rapidly enlarging mass, t(8;14) driving MYC, a starry-sky pattern on node biopsy, and a very high proliferation fraction. It is CD5 negative and would not present as an indolent 3-month lymphocytosis in a 68-year-old.
wrongExplanations.2: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma would be the answer with sheets of LARGE transformed cells on biopsy and a rapidly growing mass, often with B symptoms. It is CD5 negative in most cases and does not typically produce a circulating lymphocytosis of small mature cells.
wrongExplanations.3: Follicular lymphoma would be the answer with t(14;18) driving BCL2 and a CD10-positive, CD5-NEGATIVE phenotype in a nodular growth pattern. The CD5 positivity here excludes it.
wrongExplanations.4: Hairy cell leukemia would be the answer with splenomegaly and PANCYTOPENIA rather than lymphocytosis, a dry marrow tap, cells with fine cytoplasmic projections, and expression of CD11c, CD25, and CD103. Lymphadenopathy is characteristically absent.
wrongExplanations.5: Mantle cell lymphoma is the near-miss — the OTHER CD5-positive B-cell neoplasm. It is flipped by exactly two results, both of which point the other way here: it would be CD23 NEGATIVE and would express cyclin D1 from t(11;14).

questions.eli5: His white cells are a single cloned family of B cells that are wearing a marker normally found on a different cell type. Only two cancers do that, so one extra marker tells them apart. The fragile cells that smash on the glass slide are another clue pointing to the milder of the two.

questions.stem:
A 14-year-old boy is admitted to the hospital for treatment of newly diagnosed T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia. His leukocyte count on admission is 220,000/mm3, and a CT scan shows a bulky mediastinal mass. Induction chemotherapy is begun. Forty-eight hours after the first dose he has decreased urine output, muscle cramps, and perioral tingling. His temperature is 37.2°C (99.0°F), pulse is 104/min, and blood pressure is 108/70 mm Hg. Physical examination shows carpopedal spasm on inflation of a blood pressure cuff. Laboratory studies show:

    Serum potassium                             6.4 mEq/L
    Serum phosphorus                            8.2 mg/dL
    Serum calcium                               6.8 mg/dL
    Serum uric acid                             14.2 mg/dL
    Serum creatinine                            2.4 mg/dL (baseline 0.7)
    Prothrombin time                            12 sec (N=11–14)
    Activated partial thromboplastin time       31 sec (N=25–35)
    Fibrinogen                                  320 mg/dL (N=200–400)

Which of the following is the most likely explanation for these findings?
choices: B. Massive release of intracellular contents from lysed tumor cells
C. Renal infiltration by leukemic cells
D. Sepsis with acute tubular necrosis
E. Toxicity of the chemotherapeutic agent to the renal tubules
questions.explanation: Three values UP and one DOWN, within 48 hours of starting chemotherapy for a bulky, rapidly dividing tumor, is tumor lysis syndrome. Read it as plumbing: dying cells spill their contents into the blood. Potassium is the dominant intracellular cation → hyperkalemia. Nucleic acids are catabolized to urate → hyperuricemia, and urate crystals obstruct the tubules → acute kidney injury. Phosphate is released in large amounts → hyperphosphatemia, and the excess phosphate binds serum calcium into calcium phosphate → hypoCALCEMIA, which is why calcium is the only value that falls and why he has cramps, perioral tingling, and a positive Trousseau sign. His risk was predictable from the outset: a leukocyte count of 220,000/mm3 with bulky disease is exactly the profile that warrants prophylaxis with hydration and a urate-lowering agent BEFORE the first dose.

wrongExplanations.0: Disseminated intravascular coagulation is the common confusion, and it is excluded explicitly here. It is a COAGULOPATHY — it would require a prolonged PT and aPTT with a falling fibrinogen, and all three are normal. It also does not produce this electrolyte pattern.
wrongExplanations.2: Renal infiltration by leukemic cells can impair renal function, but it develops over a longer period and would not produce hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hyperuricemia, and hypocalcemia in a coordinated pattern 48 hours after the first dose.
wrongExplanations.3: Sepsis with acute tubular necrosis would be the answer with fever, hypotension, and a septic source. He is afebrile and normotensive, and acute tubular necrosis does not explain the profound hyperuricemia or the reciprocal phosphate-calcium relationship.
wrongExplanations.4: Direct tubular toxicity would be the answer with an agent such as cisplatin, and would characteristically cause magnesium and potassium WASTING — a LOW potassium. His potassium is high, which points to release from cells rather than loss through tubules.

questions.eli5: The chemotherapy killed a huge number of cancer cells all at once, and everything that was inside them poured into the bloodstream. Potassium, phosphate, and a waste chemical called urate all shot up, and the urate clogged his kidneys. The phosphate grabbed his calcium and pulled it down, which is why his muscles are cramping.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man is being followed after treatment for stage IIA classical Hodgkin lymphoma. His regimen consisted of doxorubicin, bleomycin, vinblastine, and dacarbazine, completed 4 months ago. He now comes to the office because of a 6-week history of a dry cough and shortness of breath on exertion. He does not smoke cigarettes and has had no fever, chest pain, or leg swelling. His temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse is 92/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 122/76 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 91%. Auscultation of the chest shows fine bibasilar inspiratory crackles. Cardiac examination shows no murmurs or gallops, and there is no jugular venous distention or peripheral edema. A chest x-ray shows bilateral reticular opacities in the lower lung fields. Echocardiography shows a left ventricular ejection fraction of 62%. Which of the following agents is the most likely cause of these findings?
questions.explanation: Predict the toxicity from the agent, and let the negatives eliminate the competitors. Bleomycin's dose-limiting toxicity is pulmonary fibrosis: it generates free radicals in lung tissue, and the lung is relatively deficient in bleomycin hydrolase, the enzyme that inactivates the drug elsewhere. The clinical picture matches exactly — a subacute dry cough, exertional dyspnea, hypoxemia, fine basilar inspiratory crackles, and reticular opacities at the lung bases weeks to months after exposure. The examination and echocardiogram deliberately close the other door in this regimen: an ejection fraction of 62% with no jugular venous distention, no gallop, and no edema rules out the anthracycline cardiomyopathy that would otherwise explain dyspnea and basilar crackles in the same patient.

wrongExplanations.1: Dacarbazine's characteristic toxicities are severe nausea and vomiting and myelosuppression. It is not associated with pulmonary fibrosis.
wrongExplanations.2: Doxorubicin is the near-miss — it is in this regimen and it does cause dyspnea and crackles, but through a dilated cardiomyopathy from anthracycline cardiotoxicity. That requires a REDUCED ejection fraction, and it would come with jugular venous distention, a gallop, and edema. His ejection fraction is 62% and all three signs are explicitly absent.
wrongExplanations.3: Vinblastine's dose-limiting toxicity is neuropathy from disruption of microtubules in axons (and myelosuppression). It would be the answer with distal sensory loss, paresthesias, or loss of deep tendon reflexes, not with an interstitial lung process.

questions.eli5: One of his four cancer drugs is known for scarring the lungs, and scarred lungs make a dry cough, low oxygen, and crackly sounds at the bases. Another drug in the same combination weakens the heart, which can look the same from the outside. The heart ultrasound came back normal, so the lungs are the answer.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man in the intensive care unit undergoes placement of a central venous catheter in the LEFT internal jugular vein for administration of vasopressors. The operator notes that two passes with the dilator were required. A chest x-ray obtained immediately after the procedure shows the catheter tip in the superior vena cava, no pneumothorax, and clear lung fields. He receives enteral tube feedings overnight. The following morning he has increasing dyspnea and a rising oxygen requirement. A repeat chest x-ray shows a large left pleural effusion. Thoracentesis yields 900 mL of opaque milky white fluid with a triglyceride concentration of 240 mg/dL. Which of the following structures was most likely injured during the procedure?
questions.explanation: Milky white pleural fluid with a triglyceride concentration above 110 mg/dL is chyle, and chyle comes from one structure. The thoracic duct drains lymph from the entire body below the diaphragm plus the left side above it, and it terminates by entering the POSTERIOR wall of the venous system at the junction of the left subclavian and left internal jugular veins — precisely the target of a left internal jugular puncture. This is why left-sided internal jugular and subclavian access carries a risk the right side does not. Two features make the timing diagnostic: the duct is thin-walled and low-pressure, so the DILATOR rather than the needle usually does the damage, and the immediate chest film looks NORMAL because chyle only accumulates once enteral feeding loads the duct with fat — the chylothorax appears the next morning, exactly as it did here.

wrongExplanations.0: Brachiocephalic vein injury would produce a hemothorax or a mediastinal hematoma with bloody, not milky, fluid, and it would typically declare itself immediately rather than overnight.
wrongExplanations.1: Phrenic nerve injury would cause an elevated left hemidiaphragm with paradoxical motion on sniff testing and no pleural fluid at all.
wrongExplanations.2: Subclavian artery injury would produce brisk pulsatile bleeding at the time of the procedure and a hemothorax, with blood in the pleural space and a falling hemoglobin.
wrongExplanations.3: Parietal pleural injury would cause a pneumothorax, which is what the immediate post-procedure chest x-ray was obtained to exclude — and it explicitly showed none. It would also not produce fluid with a triglyceride content.

questions.eli5: There is a large lymph vessel that empties into a vein on the left side of the neck, right where the catheter went in. It got nicked, and lymph fluid leaked into the chest. It only showed up the next morning because the fluid turns milky and builds up once feeding starts.

questions.stem:
A 54-year-old woman is admitted to the hospital because of a proximal deep venous thrombosis of the left leg. Warfarin is begun at a high loading dose. No parenteral anticoagulant is administered. She has received no heparin at any point. On hospital day 4 she develops a painful, sharply demarcated area of purple discoloration over the right breast that progresses over several hours to a central black eschar. Her temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse is 88/min, and blood pressure is 126/78 mm Hg. Laboratory studies show:

    Platelet count                  210,000/mm3
    International normalized ratio  3.2
    Fibrinogen                      340 mg/dL (N=200–400)

Which of the following best explains this complication?
choices: A. Antibodies directed against platelet factor 4
B. Depletion of protein C before depletion of the procoagulant factors
C. Direct cytotoxic injury to dermal capillary endothelium by warfarin
D. Immune complex deposition within dermal vessels
E. Inhibition of tissue plasminogen activator release
questions.explanation: Warfarin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase, so it blocks every vitamin K-dependent protein — the procoagulant factors II, VII, IX, and X, AND the natural anticoagulants protein C and protein S. Which effect appears first is decided entirely by half-life. Protein C has a half-life of about 8 hours, comparable to factor VII, while factor II (prothrombin) lasts roughly 60–72 hours. So in the first days of therapy protein C activity collapses while prothrombin is still largely intact → a transient PROTHROMBOTIC state → microvascular thrombosis in subcutaneous fat, producing the sharply demarcated painful necrosis seen here, classically over fatty tissue such as the breast, thigh, or buttock. A high loading dose deepens the effect, and the risk is greatest in patients with underlying protein C or S deficiency. This is the same mechanism that explains why warfarin cannot be started alone and must be bridged with a parenteral anticoagulant, and why the rising international normalized ratio — which mostly reflects factor VII — overstates how anticoagulated she actually is.

wrongExplanations.0: Antibodies against platelet factor 4 cause heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, which is excluded twice over: she has received no heparin, and her platelet count is a normal 210,000/mm3. That diagnosis requires a fall of more than 50% on day 5–10 of heparin exposure.
wrongExplanations.2: A direct cytotoxic effect on endothelium would be the answer if the lesion were dose-related, appeared at any time during therapy, and were unrelated to the anticoagulant proteins. Warfarin has no such direct toxicity — its entire action is on vitamin K recycling in the liver.
wrongExplanations.3: Immune complex deposition would be the answer for a leukocytoclastic vasculitis, which produces palpable purpura, typically on the lower extremities, often with fever, arthralgias, and renal or gastrointestinal involvement, rather than a single sharply demarcated infarct progressing to eschar.
wrongExplanations.4: Inhibition of tissue plasminogen activator release is not a warfarin effect. Impaired fibrinolysis would allow existing clot to persist but would not generate the acute microvascular thrombosis that produces skin necrosis.

questions.eli5: Warfarin switches off both the proteins that make clots and the proteins that prevent them. The braking proteins wear off within hours while the clotting proteins last for days, so the first few days of treatment actually make clotting MORE likely. Tiny clots formed in the skin and killed the tissue.
